summary: RPL normally routes packets hop by hop along a DODAG, which may not be efficient. This document lets the root install routing state to improve paths. It updates RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 8138.

eli5.summary: Instead of each sensor guessing the way, the boss hands out directions that skip detours.

questions: what is a projected dao in rpl
what is a p-route in rpl
what is a track in rpl
how does the rpl root install routes
subtitle: How a RPL Root can project shortcut and backup routes into a low-power mesh instead of making every packet detour through the Root.

tldr.problem: RPL forces node-to-node traffic along the DODAG, so in Non-Storing Mode packets go up to the Root and back down with a long Source Routing Header, which wastes bandwidth and makes the Root a bottleneck and single point of failure.
tldr.mechanism: The Root, or a Path Computation Element behind it, computes better paths and installs them with a new Projected DAO (P-DAO) message that carries a Via Information Option, as either hop-by-hop Storing Mode segments or source-routed Non-Storing Mode protection paths, grouped into a Track.
tldr.outcome: Tracks give shortcuts, shorter source routes and redundant paths that take precedence over the default route, and nodes can ask the Root for one with a P-DAO Request.

today: RFC 9914 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2026, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 8138.

sections.title: Why the Root Needs to Project Routes
sections.content:
RPL is a distance vector routing protocol for low-energy Internet of Things networks whose constrained nodes cannot keep a full view of the topology, so stretched paths are acceptable. It builds a DODAG (Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graph) whose Root often acts as the border router to the backbone. Packets follow the graph up toward the Root or down toward destinations.

That has a cost. In Non-Storing Mode every packet between two nodes goes up to the Root, which then adds a Source Routing Header (SRH) with the full path down. The header grows with the depth of the network, the bandwidth near the Root becomes the limit for all traffic, and the Root is a single point of failure. Larger packets cost energy and raise the chance of loss and fragmentation. The RFC adds that RPL is not a good fit for use cases that need high availability and reliability, because those need both short and diverse paths.

The RFC's answer is to let an abstract Path Computation Element (PCE), located in a central controller or alongside the Root, compute extra paths, and to let the Root project them into the network as Projected Routes (P-Routes). It updates RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 8138. It assumes a pre-existing main RPL Instance operating in Non-Storing Mode.
sections.eli5: In a big building where every visitor must check in at the front desk before going anywhere, the front desk gets jammed. Here the desk manager can hand out special passes so people can go straight to where they are going.

sections.title: P-Routes, Segments and Tracks
sections.content:
A P-Route is a route computed remotely by the PCE and installed and kept up by the RPL Root on its behalf. It is installed as state saying that destinations (Targets) are reachable via a sequence of nodes. The message that installs it is a Projected DAO (P-DAO).

There are two kinds. A segment is a strict, hop-by-hop path installed in Storing Mode, so each router on it keeps state. A protection path is a loose source-routed path installed in Non-Storing Mode, where only the ingress keeps state and encapsulates packets with an SRH. A Track is a set of P-Routes that forms a DODAG with its own RPL Instance and its own routing table (RIB). The Track ingress is the root of that DODAG, and it is identified by the pair (DODAGID, TrackID). Loose hops of a protection path are joined by segments or by other Tracks, and the RFC calls this stitching.

Three simple uses follow. P-Routes can be stand-alone segments that shorten the SRH for downward traffic. They can give a direct node-to-node path that avoids the Root. Or they can be combined into a Complex Track with several protection paths for redundancy. The RFC's worked example builds a path from node A to node E through B, C and D, reaching external Targets F and G, in several ways with stitched segments, external routes and segment routing.

Two strict orders prevent loops when several topologies coexist. Forwarding methods are ordered: direct neighbor, indirect neighbor via a common neighbor, segment, then nested Track, and a method may only use lower-order ones. RPL Instances are also ordered: an Instance may use another as an underlay only if that one is a descendant of it in the graph of Instances, with the main Instance as the top. A packet that was forwarded along a Track MUST NOT be forwarded along the default route of the main Instance.
sections.eli5: Think of the main road network as the normal way everyone drives. A segment is a short bypass with signs at every turn. A protection path is a written list of towns to pass through. A Track is the whole bundle of bypasses and lists that the road manager built for one trip.

sections.title: New Messages and Options
sections.content:
The P-DAO is an ordinary DAO message with a new P flag in bit position 2 of the Flags field. Only the Root may send it, sourced from its address that is the DODAGID of the main DODAG, and receivers MUST silently ignore a P-DAO not sent by the Root. It also carries a TrackID and a DODAGID field holding the address of the Track ingress. The matching acknowledgment is the P-DAO-ACK.

A P-DAO contains one or more RPL Target Options (the Targets reached) followed by exactly one Via Information Option (VIO), which lists the ordered via addresses. An SM-VIO (option type 0x0F) is a strict Storing Mode path. An NSM-VIO (option type 0x10) is a loose Non-Storing Mode path. The VIO also holds a P-RouteID (the segment or protection path ID), a Segment Sequence whose initial value is 255 and which decides which update is fresher, and a Segment Lifetime in which 255 means infinity and 0 means reachability is lost. In an NSM-VIO the list excludes the ingress and ends at the Track egress, which is an implicit Target and MUST NOT be listed in a Target Option.

A node can ask for a Track with a P-DAO Request (P-DAO-REQ, control code 0x09). It has a TrackID, a K flag asking for an acknowledgment, an R flag asking for a redundant Complex Track, a ReqLifetime where 255 means infinity and 0 destroys the Track, and a PDRSequence. The Root answers with a PDR-ACK (control code 0x0A) that echoes the sequence and carries the remaining Track Lifetime and a status.

The Sibling Information Option (SIO, option type 0x11) lets a node tell the Root about neighbors that are usable but were not used to form the main DODAG, so the PCE can build paths through them. A B flag says the link is roughly symmetrical, and a Step in Rank field gives the cost.

Three smaller changes support the data plane and signaling. The RPL Option (the RPI) gets a P flag that is set when a packet is sent over a Track. 6LoWPAN gets a new routing header, the P-RPI-6LoRH, with type value 8. The DODAG Configuration option gets a D flag ("Projected Routes Support") in bit position 0, which tells nodes that the Root will install requested Tracks.
sections.eli5: There is now a special note that only the boss may write, saying 'to reach these places, pass through these stops.' Helpers can also send the boss a request form for a new route, and tell the boss which neighbors they can talk to directly.

sections.title: Installing, Maintaining and Removing Tracks
sections.content:
A Storing Mode P-DAO goes to the segment egress, the last node on the path. Each node passes it unchanged to its predecessor in the via list, from egress back to ingress, and every node except the egress installs a route to the Targets via its successor. The ingress replies with a P-DAO-ACK to the Root. A router that cannot store the routes rejects it with "Out of Resources", and one that cannot reach its predecessor rejects it with "Predecessor Unreachable". The egress answers "Unreachable Target" if it does not know a Target.

A Non-Storing Mode P-DAO goes to the Track ingress, which builds a tunnel for the Targets and MUST use the NSM-VIO content verbatim as the Routing Header when it encapsulates. Because each loose hop must be reachable, nested P-Routes must be installed first and P-Routes must be installed from last to first along the datapath. A segment must exist before the protection path that uses it.

Priority and bookkeeping rules keep this safe. The longest match is the prime comparison for routing, and for an equal-length match a route along a Track MUST be preferred over one along the main DODAG. A VIO MUST contain at least one via address and none may appear twice, since that would create a loop. A node MAY check for this, and if it finds a problem it MUST reject with "Error in VIO".

To request a Track, a node picks an unused TrackID and sends a P-DAO-REQ to the Root, which MAY install it. To avoid collisions the RFC recommends that the ingress allocates TrackID values starting at 0 and counting up, while the Root starts at 63 and counts down. A node should resend its request about one trip time before the lifetime ends, or the Root tears down the Track. A "Transient Failure" status means retry later, and any other negative status is permanent until corrected.

To remove a route, the Root sends a P-DAO with a Segment Lifetime of 0, a No-Path P-DAO, and a newer sequence. To change a path without losing packets, the Root installs the new section from its last node to its first, then removes the old section after a reasonable time so in-flight packets drain. When it adds a protection path, the Root should install it before removing a failing one, since dropping a Track first would reroute traffic through the Root.
sections.eli5: To build a shortcut the boss starts at the destination end and tells each stop along the way, one after another back to the start, so that nobody is pointed at a road that is not finished yet. To close it, the boss sends a 'forget this road' note the same way.

sections.title: Forwarding Along a Track
sections.content:
When a Track ingress puts a packet on a Track, it encapsulates it with IP-in-IP, adding a Routing Header and a Hop-by-Hop header with the RPI. The outer source address is the Track DODAGID, and the RPI carries the TrackID, with the DODAGID flag in the RPLInstanceID set to 0. No encapsulation is needed when the ingress itself originated the packet and the egress is its destination. For a local RPL Instance the TrackID is a number the RFC expresses as 128 to 191.

Each router handles a packet in a fixed order. If the packet is for itself, it follows any unfinished Source Routing Header, otherwise decapsulates and recurses, or delivers it. If not, the router forwards to a direct neighbor, else to an indirect neighbor through a common neighbor, else along a RIB entry for the same Track, else by encapsulating into a different Track, else drops it. A packet that has left a Track MUST NOT be routed along the default route of the main DODAG, because the end-to-end path would no longer be controlled.

A node that drops a packet this way MUST send an ICMPv6 error to the Root with the new code "Error in P-Route", throttled and sourced from the address used in the Track, so the Root can repair the segment or Track. In 6LoWPAN networks the RPL artifacts are compressed with RFC 8138: the SRH-6LoRH is copied from the VIO, the P-RPI-6LoRH carries the TrackID, and an IP-in-IP 6LoRH carries the Track DODAGID.

Because encapsulation adds headers, the RFC recommends an MTU larger than 1280 between RPL routers while still exposing 1280 to endpoint stacks, to limit fragmentation.
sections.eli5: Packets going on a shortcut get put inside a bigger envelope that has the route written on it. When they reach the end of the shortcut the outer envelope is opened. If a stop finds the next road is missing, it throws the packet away and tells the boss so the boss can fix it.

sections.title: Profiles and Compatibility
sections.content:
Because implementations rarely need everything, the RFC defines profiles 0 to 9. Profiles 0 to 2 work in the main Instance and need no Local RPL Instance support. Profile 0 is legacy Non-Storing Mode, and Profile 1 uses Storing Mode segments to shorten the SRH. Profiles 0 and 1 are REQUIRED for all implementations that may be used in LLNs. Profile 2, which uses Non-Storing Mode P-Routes along the main DODAG, is RECOMMENDED in high-speed environments such as wired ones. All other profile and environment combinations are OPTIONAL. Profiles 3 and above use Local RPL Instances to build arbitrary Tracks. Profile 7 runs on a Storing Mode main DODAG, and Profiles 8 and 9 give the Track ingress a full DODAG view in preparation for the RAW work.

The RFC expects a Non-Storing Mode main DODAG because the Root already knows the topology and reaches nodes with unicast messages. A less constrained variation for a Storing Mode main DODAG is described: nodes must send extra unicast DAOs to the Root that carry SIOs, since the Root otherwise lacks child-to-parent and sibling information. A Track can also be sent to the ingress as a full DODAG using Targets and Transit Information Options.

For backward compatibility, a node that does not understand the new P-DAO-REQ discards it, and all nodes that need to process a P-DAO MUST support the RFC. The Root should set the D flag in DIO messages only when all the nodes that could be on a Track path have been upgraded. How the Root learns node capabilities, how the PCE computes paths and which protocol links the PCE to the Root are all out of scope.
sections.eli5: Not every device needs every trick, so the RFC makes a menu of packages. Two basic ones are must-haves for tiny networks. The boss should only announce that shortcuts are available once all the stops on the way know how to follow them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC reuses messages already in RPL, with their optional secured versions, so whatever security a network uses applies here as well. Every node in the LLN is RPL-aware and could inject an attack. A trust model is therefore needed to be sure the right devices act as Root and as RPL-aware nodes, to avoid sinkhole attacks. At a minimum it could rest on layer-2 secure joining and link-layer security, and the RFC mentions the 6TiSCH Constrained Join Protocol as an example.

Only the Root may generate P-DAO messages, and P-DAO-REQ messages MUST be sent to the Root. The RFC expects communication with the Root to be authenticated, without choosing a method. Link-layer security is needed to stop a rogue router from forging P-DAOs to cause high churn and use up the storage in routers.

The checks the RFC adds, such as rejecting a VIO that lists a node twice, are only minimal protection. An attacker who can inject P-DAOs could reroute any traffic and quickly drain scarce resources such as spectrum and battery.
sections.eli5: If anyone could write signs on the shortcuts, a trickster could send all the traffic to the wrong place. So only the real boss may do it, and the network must check that the boss is really the boss.

fields.name: K
fields.desc: Set to ask the Root for a PDR-ACK.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Set to request a redundant Complex Track.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Reserved; set to zero and ignored.

fields.name: ReqLifetime
fields.desc: Requested lifetime; 255 is infinity, 0 destroys the Track.

fields.name: PDRSequence
fields.desc: Wrapping sequence number echoed in the PDR-ACK.
